title: Concrete Patio vs Pavers: Cost and Lifespan
description: Concrete costs less up front at $5 to $15 per sq ft, pavers cost $10 to $17 but repair one piece at a time. Compare cost and lifespan here.

cover.alt: Illustration of a balance scale on a outdoor & yard blueprint background with a measuring tape

takeaways: Poured concrete costs $5 to $15 per sq ft installed, while pavers cost $10 to $17 per sq ft installed.
Angi puts concrete lifespan at 30 to 50 years and brick pavers at 25 to 35 years, with care changing both numbers a lot.
Pick pavers if you want easy spot repairs, and pick concrete if you want the lowest first price on a flat site.
body:
Poured concrete is cheaper up front, and pavers are easier to repair later. For most homes, concrete costs $5 to $15 per sq ft installed and pavers cost $10 to $17 per sq ft installed, so pick concrete for a low first price on a flat yard and pick pavers if you want to replace single pieces instead of cutting out a slab.

## The direct cost and lifespan comparison

HomeGuide lists a poured concrete patio at $5 to $15 per sq ft installed and a concrete or brick paver patio at $10 to $17 per sq ft installed. Angi lists the same split in its patio guide, with concrete at $3 to $8 per sq ft for the material type table and a longer life range. Use the installed HomeGuide range for budgeting, because it covers labor and base work.

| Item | Poured concrete | Pavers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Installed cost per sq ft | $5 to $15 | $10 to $17 |
| Cost for 400 sq ft (20 x 20 ft) | $2,000 to $6,000 | $4,000 to $6,800 |
| Lifespan from Angi table | 30 to 50 years | 25 to 35 years for brick pavers |
| Repair style | Patch, resurface, or cut out a section | Lift and replace single pieces |
| Look | One smooth slab, stamped options cost more | Many colors, shapes, and patterns |
| Ground movement | Cracks show in the slab | Joints flex, pieces can be relevelled |
| DIY fit | Hard, one fast pour | Slow but forgiving, base work is heavy |

Stamped concrete sits between the two on price. HomeGuide puts stamped concrete at $8 to $19 per sq ft installed. It looks like stone or brick, but you still get one slab that can crack as one slab.

Lifespan needs care in how you read it. Angi notes concrete pavers at 25 to 50 years in its paver guide. A patio fails first at the base, joints, and edges, so a well built base helps both surfaces last.

## Worked example: a 16 x 20 ft patio

Say your patio is 16 x 20 ft (4.9 x 6.1 m), big enough for a table, six chairs, and a grill.

Step 1, area. 16 ft x 20 ft = 320 sq ft.

Step 2, concrete cost. Low end: 320 x $5 = $1,600. Typical mid point at $10 per sq ft: 320 x $10 = $3,200. High end: 320 x $15 = $4,800.

Step 3, paver cost. Low end: 320 x $10 = $3,200. Typical mid point at $13.50 per sq ft: 320 x $13.50 = $4,320. High end: 320 x $17 = $5,440.

Step 4, check the math a second way. For 100 sq ft, concrete at $10 is $1,000. For 320 sq ft, that is 3.2 x $1,000 = $3,200, which matches Step 2. For pavers at $13.50, 100 sq ft is $1,350, and 3.2 x $1,350 = $4,320, which matches Step 3.

So on this size, pavers cost about $1,120 more than concrete at the typical mid points. That gap pays for the base gravel, sand, edging, and the labor to lay each piece. If you plan the paver layout, our [paver calculator](/blog/paver-calculator/) shows pavers, base gravel, and sand for your exact size.

## What changes the price for each one?

For concrete, thickness, finish, and access move the price. A plain broom finish on a flat, open yard sits near the low end. Stamping, color, extra thickness, a pump truck for a tight yard, and removal of an old patio push the price up. Ask if the quote covers a gravel base, wire mesh or rebar, control joints, and sealing.

For pavers, the paver itself is only part of the bill. Base gravel depth, sand, edge restraints, cuts for curves, and steps or a sitting wall add cost. A simple rectangle in a common running bond pattern costs less than a circle or a herringbone field with a border. Local stone costs more to haul than concrete pavers made near you.

Site work hits both prices. Grading, a drain line, and removal of roots or old concrete all add money. Get site work as its own line so you can compare bids fairly.

## How do repairs and upkeep compare?

Concrete needs little day to day care. Sweep it, wash it, and seal it every few years if your installer advises it. Hairline cracks are normal. A wide crack, a lifted corner, or a sunken section is harder to fix well, and a patch rarely matches the old color. Cutting out and repouring one section can leave a visible square.

Pavers need joint care. Sand in the joints washes out over time, weeds grow in open joints, and one low paver can hold water. The fix is local. Lift the low pieces, add or level the sand bed, set them back, and sweep in new joint sand. Angi advises resealing pavers every 3 to 5 years and adding sand every 5 to 10 years. That upkeep is simple, but you have to do it.

In cold states, water under a slab can lift it. Pavers flex a bit with the ground, so they often handle small shifts with less visible damage.

## Pick this if: the clear verdict

Pick concrete if your yard is flat, your budget is tight, and you want a clean slab fast. It is also the better pick for a large plain area where pattern adds little, such as a side yard pad or a base for a shed or hot tub, if the slab is built for that load.

Pick pavers if you want pattern and color, if your soil shifts, or if you plan to run a wire or pipe under the patio later. You can lift pavers, do the work, and set them back the same day. That one trait saves real money over 20 years on many lots.

Pick stamped concrete only if you love the look and accept slab repairs. It costs close to pavers, so compare a stamped quote and a paver quote side by side before you sign. For a deck instead of a patio, see our guide to the [cost to build a deck](/blog/cost-to-build-a-deck/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a concrete patio cheaper than pavers for 320 sq ft?
Yes. At HomeGuide installed rates, concrete runs $1,600 to $4,800 for 320 sq ft and pavers run $3,200 to $5,440. The typical gap in our worked example was about $1,120.

### How long does a concrete patio last compared with pavers?
Angi puts concrete at 30 to 50 years and brick pavers at 25 to 35 years. Good base work, drainage, and joint care can push a paver patio well past its low end, and poor base work can shorten a slab life.

### Do pavers need sealing?
Sealing is optional for many pavers, but Angi suggests resealing every 3 to 5 years to hold color and help joints. Unsealed pavers still work, they just fade faster and stain more easily.

### Can you put pavers over old concrete?
You can on a sound, flat slab with good drainage, using thin overlay pavers. If the slab is cracked from soil movement or holds water, remove it and build a proper base, or the new surface will show the same faults.

### Which patio is better for DIY?
Pavers are the safer DIY pick for most people. The work is heavy and slow, but you can fix a mistake the same day. A concrete pour is one fast job with no pause, so most patios are better left to a crew. Start with our [gravel calculator](/blog/gravel-calculator/) for the base amount either way.

### Do you need a permit for a patio?
Many towns need a permit for a concrete patio, and rules vary by town and size. Pavers on a gravel base often need no permit, but check setback and drainage rules with your town before you dig.
